lignes.texte: Most of what you learned in geography class… is a lie.
Millions of people confidently repeat facts about continents, cities and what can be
seen from space. And honestly, they’re probably closer to fiction than reality.
Ask anyone how many continents there are in the world… and the answer is probably wrong.
Depending on where you grew up, you were taught there are 5, 6 or 7 continents. Some countries
teach that the Americas are one whole continent. Others teach that Eurasia is one continent.
But even if you were taught that there are 7,
your teachers probably still lied to you. Because there’s an entire continent hidden from view.
Welcome to Zealandia.
It’s 1.65 times larger than India. But 94% of its landmass is submerged underwater. The biggest
pieces poking out from the ocean’s surface? The islands of New Caledonia and New Zealand.
Speaking of islands…
Indonesia is the country with the most islands in the world. Or maybe
it’s the Philippines. Those are the two most frequent guesses among the general public.
And they’re both wrong.
The crown belongs to Sweden, pacing over 267,000 islands spread across its territory. Its Nordic
neighbors, Norway and Finland, aren’t too far behind with 150,000 islands. Massive chunks
of these countries exist as archipelagos, carved out by glacial retreats during the last Ice Age.
By comparison, Indonesia only has around 17,500, while the Philippines have 7,600.
And since we’re in Scandinavia…
Most people confuse Nordic and Scandinavian countries,
which explains why Finland usually gets called “Scandinavian”...
Even though it’s not.
The real Scandinavian countries are Denmark,
Sweden, and Norway. They all share closer linguistic, cultural,
and historic ties with each other than they do with neighboring Finland. The Finnish language
shares zero roots with them and its people come from completely different ethnic origins.
However, Finland, as well as Iceland,
is part of the Nordics. All 5 countries do share some political and cultural ties.
Moving one over to Norway…
People usually think Norway is the northernmost country in the world because
the northernmost permanently inhabited town in the world is there. But Russia,
Canada, and Greenland all reach further towards the North Pole.
The actual northernmost country in the world? Denmark. It’s all thanks to a peninsula of
Kaffeklubben Island, a slice of land sitting off the coast of its autonomous territory, Greenland.
What about the other side of the world?
Not only do many people believe that the South Pole is always by definition
located in Antarctica; many even use the South Pole and Antarctica interchangeably.
But the South Pole isn’t just one thing.
There’s the Geographic South Pole, which is where the earth’s axis intersects Earth’s
crust. Then there’s the Geomagnetic South Pole, where the geomagnetic field intersects
the Earth’s surface. Then the Magnetic South Pole, where Earth’s magnetic fields intersect
the crust. This pole isn’t even constant. It’s perpetually moving around. And, of course,
there’s the Pole of Inaccessibility, where Antarctica is farthest from any nearby shoreline.
Antarctica actually has many myths surrounding it.
While several regions in Antarctica don’t have time zones, that’s not
true across the whole continent. 7 countries have territorial claims in
Antarctica and operate numerous research stations that rely on time zones to work.
Each station adjusts its time zone to its country of origin, or to their supply base. That way,
they can communicate with their headquarters most effectively.
Not that time zones always make sense to begin with…
A common belief is that Time zones are constructed based
on longitude. And that’s true for most places.
But some countries like to mess it up.
Take Spain, for example. It should be in the same time zone as London,
as it sits underneath it. It’d make sense for both of them to be on GMT time. Except,
Spain is one hour ahead… all because of one man’s decision.
Dictator Francisco Franco.
He wanted to show support for Hitler during WWII - without
actually joining the war - so he decided to change Spain’s time zone
to match Germany’s. Despite Germany being significantly to the east of the country.
When Franco died decades later,
Spanish people had become used to the new time zone, so decided to keep it.
There’s general time zone confusion all around though…
Russia is so big it’s larger than Pluto, it would make sense for it to have the most
time zones of any country. But that’s not the case. Because while Russia has 11 time zones,
another country managed to sneak ahead and get 12.
France.
The extraordinary amount of time zones is due to the country’s overseas territories,
including French Polynesia, Reunion, and French Guiana,
to name just a few. Other former colonist countries also have an unexpectedly large
number of time zones due to remaining territories; the UK still has 9.
Any idea what the closest country to Madagascar is? Mozambique maybe?
Incorrect, even though it may see that way on the map. The closest country to Madagascar is…France.
And it’s all down to those overseas territories again.
Northwest of Madagascar is the small island of Mayotte. And it
is officially - and has been since 1841 - an overseas department and territory of France.
It just shows that our mental map doesn’t always make sense…
Greenland seems like it's west of Iceland.
But that’s a geographic illusion.
The frozen giant is so huge, it actually stretches further west, north, east, and south than Iceland.
The eastern peninsula, known as Northern Foreland,
or Nordostrundingen locally, reaches so far across, it hangs over Iceland.
Turns out, figuring out east and west is harder than people think…
It seems like common sense to say Maine is the easternmost state in
the U.S. When you look at a map of the United States, Maine is clearly
furthest east. But most people don’t take the International Date Line into account.
Alaska’s Aleutian islands cross over the 180th meridian, putting
them in the eastern hemisphere. Making Alaska the country’s easternmost state.
Alaska has other myths surrounding it, like…
Alaska is so big, it dwarfs African nations like Libya Algeria or the
Democratic Republic of the Congo. The map doesn’t lie afterall. Except it does.
Alaska is smaller than all of these countries.
The Mercator Map projection has been lying to us for years. Because the globe is stretched
out flat to create most maps today, landmasses further away from the equator get distorted to
appear much larger than they are. Meanwhile, the opposite happens for those closer to the equator.
But most people still don’t understand just how bad the distortion is.
Libya is 19% larger than Alaska. The DRC is 59% larger, and Algeria is 61% larger .
To get a true idea of the size of something though, you should try viewing it from space…
Contrary to popular belief, very few things can actually be seen from space in such detail,
and that includes the Great Wall of China. Which is actually a testament to
its engineering. Because even though it’s huge, it’s relatively narrow,
and it blends into its environment and surrounding geographical contours quite well.
So can any human-made structure be seen from space? With the naked eye,
and no telephoto lens… a surprising amount can. Like the Palm Jumeirah in Dubai,
an artificial island resembling a palm sticking out into the sea. And Bingham
Canyon Mine in Utah, the biggest human-made excavation in the world.
At least one visible manmade structure in China that’s not the Great Wall,
has been seen by astronauts from space. The Three Gorges Dam,
on the Yangtze River; known as the largest power-producing facility in the world.
Oh, while we’re talking about myths and rivers…
While the Nile is certainly impressive,
and looks the longest from space, it’s not the longest river in the world.
There have been multiple studies that suggest that the much-harder-to-visually-gauge Amazon
River is longer. Because the Amazon has multiple tributaries,
and incredibly dense rainforest cover, it’s taken a much longer time to accurately
measure it down to the last inch. And the data shows that the Amazon wins… but not by much.
Just 65 miles (105 km)
But it’s enough to be crowned the longest river in the world.
Beyond record-breaking rivers, people can’t even agree on basic facts about them…
Rivers flow in one direction… or do they?
It’s not always the case. Changes in direction can be caused by anything from
temporary storm surges in the Mississippi River causing the water to back up. Or it
can be ocean tides pushing seawater up the Hudson and causing it to reverse.
The Tonle Sap in Cambodia changes its direction seasonally. Twice a year,
it completely reverses flow, mostly based on the monsoon season.
And that’s not it for unexpected directions…
If you’re in the Americas, the sun always rises in the Atlantic and sets in the Pacific.
Unless you’re in Panama. The central section of the
country bends in a way that - for a very short distance - puts the
Atlantic on its northwest coast, and the Pacific on its southeast coast. Meaning,
if you’re near the Panama Canal, the sun rises in the Pacific and sets in the Atlantic.
There’s a U.S. myth about bordering multiple oceans as well…
The east coast of Florida borders the Atlantic Ocean, while its west
coast sits on the Gulf. But that doesn’t make it the only state to touch two seas.
There’s another U.S. state that touches not just two seas, but two oceans. Alaska.
The Last Frontier’s southern coast runs along the Pacific Ocean,
while its northern coast borders the Arctic Ocean.
Alaska really is very high on the geography myth list…
When U.S. vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin said on television that Russia
is Alaska’s neighbor, it became ingrained in pop culture. Unless you’re on extremely high ground,
on an exceptionally clear day… it’s hard to see Russia from the mainland.
But… cross the water to a tiny Alaskan island and the myth becomes reality.
Standing on Little Diomede Island, Alaska, you can actually see Big Diomede Island,
Russia. The two superpowers are only 2.5 miles (4 km) apart.
But only 100 people live on Little Diomede, and Big Diomede is uninhabited except for
a Russian base. So most people will never experience that view.
Russia and Turkey are not the only transcontinental countries
despite what your geography teacher told you.
The line separating Europe from Asia cuts through the Caucasus. That means Georgia,
Azerbaijan, and even Kazakhstan in Central Asia sit on two continents.
And that’s just the start.
Egypt sits in both Asia and Africa, also making it
transcontinental. Add in non-contiguous landmasses that sit on two continents,
and France is technically in Europe, Africa, Oceania, and South America.
The list is much longer than anyone thinks.
There’s much more confusion over borders…
Denmark only shares a border with Germany.
But that changed in 2022. Since then, it also shares a border with Canada.
Denmark and Canada had spent almost 50 years fighting over a tiny spit of land
between Canada and Greenland known as Hans Island. A treaty was signed in 1973 leaving
the issue to be decided at a later date, but the tension rolled on for decades.
Eventually, in 2022, they decided the best thing to do would be to divide
Hans Island down the middle, and give each country a half.
Too bad this next issue can’t be settled so easily…
Afghanistan isn’t a Middle Eastern country.
Geographically, and according to the UN, Afghanistan sits squarely in South Asia,
along with Pakistan and India. Even geographers who disagree
on which region the country is located in put it at the crossroads of Central
Asia and South Asia. Western Asia - the actual Middle East - is never mentioned.
Unfortunately, Afghanistan likely got lumped in with the Middle East in most peoples’
minds because of the deadly war that raged in the country for years. Westerns connect the
general conflict and the Middle Eastern region, masking the country’s true Asian geography.
That’s not the only area of confusion…
Many people think Central America is part of South America. It’s a common
mistake because Central America is considered part
of Latin America. That gives it a cultural and linguistic tie to most of South America.
So when most foreigners see a bunch of Spanish-speaking countries all sharing
borders from Guatemala down to Argentina, they assume there’s some continuity there.
However, Central America is firmly part of North America.
But confusion about continents is nothing new…
South America isn’t really directly south of America.
Most of the continent - as in 99% - sits entirely east of Miami. It
sounds ridiculous… until you look at a map. At which point,
it becomes obvious. So why do our brains often think of it differently?
It’s a phenomenon known as cognitive simplification. Instead of wasting energy
on things that aren’t that useful or important in everyday life, your brain creates vague
outlines. It helps reduce complex information and environments into simple, manageable shortcuts.
Because “South” is in the name,
your mind instantly puts the entire continent below North America.
Cognitive simplification can also be amplified by other factors…
One look at the temperature and you’d think Mediterranean countries
are at the same latitude as the warmer U.S. states
They’re not.
Milan is actually north of Portland, Maine.
As ridiculous as it might sound that a major city in the sunny, Mediterranean country of
Italy could lie north of a city in one of the U.S.’ northernmost, chilliest states…it's
true. Our mental maps put Europe in the wrong place, much like they do with South America.
Europe is also much warmer than it should be because of the Gulf Stream.
So people naturally place it closer to the equator in their mental maps than it should be.
While London, England, sits at almost the same exact latitude as Calgary, Canada,
spend a winter in each place and you will experience a very different climate. The
average low temperature in January in London is 39 degrees Fahrenheit (3.9 Celsius). In
Calgary it drops down to a bone chilling 13 degrees Fahrenheit (-10.6 Celsius).
Which is why, even though it's further north, Milan is still associated with
Mediterranean summers, while Portland is associated with puffy jackets and rainboots.
There are many more myths about the Mediterranean and the countries in it though…
Portugal isn’t a Mediterranean country
You might think the opposite because Portugal sits on the same line as Spain,
Italy, and Greece. It’s also often grouped together with
them by foreigners thinking of where to take their next summer vacation.
But no part of Portugal lies on the Mediterranean Sea.
The country’s coastline is entirely on the Atlantic Ocean; which is perhaps why its
beaches are better known for surfing than crystal clear blue waters. Even though it's
geographically false, Portugal will continue to be tied to the Mediterranean because of
similarities to the other Med countries in terms of food, climate, and culture.
Ready for another Mediterranean myth…
Most people associate Greece with a summer vacation to Mykonos or Santorini,
making foreigners believe that the entire place is sandy, warm, and coastal.
But 80% of Greece is made up of mountains. The highest is Mount Olympus, made famous
through Greek mythology, which stands close to 9,600 feet (2,926 meters). Temperatures in
the country’s northern ranges regularly fall - and stay - below freezing in the winter,
and several ski and snowboard resorts operate during the cold season.
Speaking of mountains…
Europe has some pretty impressive peaks, but the highest isn’t Mont Blanc
It’s true if we’re looking solely at Western Europe,
but remember, Russia is also considered a part of Europe.
That's why Europe’s universally acknowledged highest peak is the summit of Mount Elbrus,
Russia, standing just over 18,500 feet (5,638 meters) above sea level. Even if you were to argue
that part of Russia belongs to Asia, Mount Elbrus sits squarely on the European continental plate.
Mountain climbers see it as one of the Seven Summits - the
highest peak in each of the seven continents. And they should know.
If you’re standing in a field in Nebraska, the Great Plains must
look like the flattest place on earth. No visible elevation change in any direction.
But the Great Plains are a massive area. And they change elevation. It
just happens so gradually it’s not visible to anyone standing in them.
The mile-high (1.6 km) city of Denver, Colorado is located in the Great Plains. The plains gently
slope upwards from east to west, starting from 2,000 feet (610 meters) high and eventually
reach an elevation of over 6,000 feet (,1829 meters) as they approach the Rocky Mountains.
Making the Great Plains not so flat after all.
Other surprising myths about geographic features include…
The Sahara is arguably the most famous desert in the world,
and the largest hot desert. But it hasn’t been around as long as some others.
The Namib Desert has been around for at least 55 million years.
Meanwhile, the Sahara has only been in existence for 2-3 million years at most.
In the local language, Namib name means “an area where there is nothing”. It’s one of the
most picturesque - yet also inhospitable - deserts out there. Summer temperatures
often shoot about 115 degrees Fahrenheit (46.1 Celsius) while nights plunge below freezing.
But a harsh climate and land doesn’t always mean no one lives there…
The “stan” countries - Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan,
and Kyrgyzstan - are often thought of as mostly empty nations on the steppes of Central Asia.
It’s true that the climate and landscape of most of Central Asia is very unforgiving,
leaving large parts sparsely inhabited. Kazakhstan, for example,
has a population of 20 million people while being the ninth largest country by area in the world.
But that doesn’t mean the region is empty. Kazakhstan’s cities are booming metropolises,
with 2.4 million people living in Almaty and over 1.5 million in Astana. Uzbekistan,
an especially fertile pocket of the region, has a population of 38 million people.
Overall, the Central Asian population is 85 million people as of today,
and expected to exceed 114 million people by 2050.
Which will change this next myth even more…
It’s often said that one third of the global population is in Asia
As astounding as it is to think that 33% of the entire earth’s population
is located in just one continent, the truth is even more shocking.
60% of the world’s population is in Asia.
That means if an alien were to pick a human, any human from earth,
there’s a 3 in 5 chance that person would be Asian. Considering the continent has some of
the most highly populated countries on the planet,
it should come as no surprise. But most people don’t guess that the ratio is that high.
The current population of the Asian continent is 4.7 billion people.
But where they are is shifting…
Any idea what the most populated nation in the world is?
China is the most frequent guess… and for 75 years,
that answer was 100% correct. But then the global leaderboard changed.
In April 2023, India’s rapidly growing population overtook China’s stalling one,
a decline partly due to the one child policy.
Today, China has 1.41 billion people, while India has surged to 1.48 billion.
On the topic of population upsets…
Tokyo is seen as the largest city in the world
A more accurate statement would be that Tokyo was the largest city in
the world. According to the UN, Tokyo lost that title to Jakarta in 2025.
The Indonesian capital now has 42 million residents,
compared to the Tokyo metropolitan area that currently has 37 million people.
Let’s move away from booming cities to lonely ones…
Residents of Perth, Australia, love to boast that they live in the most isolated state
capital and the most isolated city in the world. But that title belongs to Honolulu,
Hawaii, which is 2,300 miles (3,701 km) away from the nearest major city of San Francisco.
As far as the most isolated large city goes?
Large cities are generally defined as having a population over 1 million, and Perth had about
2.4 million residents. But as of 2024, Honolulu had 998,700 people in its metropolitan area,
and was growing. Meaning the population is almost certainly over 1 million now.
Making Honolulu both the most isolated state capital and large city.
From isolated cities to isolated landscapes, let’s get to…
People often name Yellowstone the biggest National Park in the U.S. While it might
definitely be one of the most famous parks, it’s not even the biggest in the lower 48 states.
That title would go to Death Valley National Park; 3.4 million acres (1.3 million hectares) to
Yellowstone’s 2.2 million acres (890,308 hectares). More than one a half times its size.
But both these parks pale in comparison to the U.S. true largest National Park:
Wrangell-St. Elias. Never heard of it? Truth is, most people, even Americans,
haven’t. Because it’s up in the Alaskan wilderness, clocking in at a massive 13.2
million acres. That’s almost twice the size of Hawaii.
Moving on to the British Isles…
Great Britain and the United Kingdom are not the same
Every person from the region probably already knows this,
but many people in the rest of the world use these names interchangeably.
But the United Kingdom is a country consisting of England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland.
Great Britain is the name given to the island which is home to England, Wales, and Scotland.
Northern Ireland is also part of the island of Ireland.
Speaking of confusing names…
Holland is an old/alternate name for the Netherlands
False.
The Netherlands is the official name of an EU country, but many people
also call it Holland. However, those terms can’t be used interchangeably.
The Netherlands has 12 provinces,
2 of which are North Holland and South Holland. So why the confusion?
Because North and South Holland are pretty important provinces,
since they include Amsterdam, Rotterdam, and the Hague. In other words, the main legislative,
financial, and trading centers of the country.
Centuries ago, traders from the Netherlands would tell foreigners they encountered they
were from “Noord Holland” or “Zuid Holland”. So the confusion began… and apparently, continued.
Sometimes people don’t confuse the name of a place, just where it came from…
New Mexico isn’t named after the country of Mexico. It’s actually the other way around.
The area now called New Mexico was called that 223 years before Mexico became an independent
country. The Spanish explorers had originally named it after Aztec lands in the area of Mexico
it reminded them of. Back then, “Mexico” was just a name for the area around the Aztec capital city.
So when Spain withdrew from its colony in 1821,
New Mexico became…part of the new independent country of Mexico.
Speaking of…
The historic city of Boston is one of the major U.S. cities most tied to the American
Revolution and the entire independence movement. And Massachusetts was one of the
original 13 colonies. So most people guess that the oldest state capital is… Boston.
And they would be wrong. Because it’s actually Sante Fe, New Mexico.
The Spanish established it in 1610. Boston wasn’t officially established until 1630.
Making Santa Fe the oldest state capital in the USA.
While the southeastern state of Florida might make
sense as being closest to Africa, the actual closest state is Maine.
At first glance, snowy Maine seems the furthest possible thing from Africa. But because the
slope of the U.S.’ eastern seaboard is much more slanted than it seems. It heads further
and further west and inland the further south it goes… leaving Maine jutting out into the Atlantic.
The peninsula of Quoddy Head, Maine, is over 3,100 miles (4,989 km) from
Morocco. Florida’s closest point to Africa is over 1,000 miles (1,6099 km) further away.
How about dispelling some African geographic facts?
Lagos is the capital of Nigeria
File this one under “used to be true, but most people didn’t catch the update”.
The capital of Nigeria was moved from Lagos to Abuja
in 1991. That was before Gen Z were even born.
Crushed by overpopulation, gridlocked traffic, and poor infrastructure, Nigerian officials decided
to abandon Lagos and establish a new capital. The government chose a place where none of the
country’s dominant ethnic groups had a stronghold, reducing the possibility of domestic infighting.
Abuja seemed like the perfect choice. Though
most Nigerians don’t think it accomplished much after all.
But there’s more capital confusion as people think…
Geneva may be the most well-known Swiss city,
as it functions as a huge financial center and tourist hub. But it’s not the Swiss capital.
No, Zurich isn’t the answer either. In fact, Switzerland technically
doesn’t have a capital. Instead, it has a “federal city” that acts like a capital…
Bern.
The reason Switzerland doesn’t have an official capital is because of the unique
way it's divided. The separate cantons theoretically should have equal power.
Putting a capital in any one of them would give that canton a privileged
status. So Switzerland decided to go with a “federal city” instead.
It’s not the only country to do its own thing regarding capitals…
Cape Town isn’t the capital of South Africa
Well, not the only one. South Africa decided to go in the opposite direction of Switzerland;
and institute three capitals instead.
Cape Town is one of them; the legislative capital. Pretoria is the administrative
capital and Bloemfontein is the judicial capital. Cape Town is probably the one that
gets named because it’s the South Africa city foreigners are most familiar with.
Strangely enough, South Africa split the system to keep the balance of
power between different South African regions. The opposite of Switzerland.
This next country is fully balanced, but the myth is that…
Most people believe that no country sits in all
four hemispheres. But Kiribati is here to prove them wrong.
The country has a population of 130,000 people and less than 6,000 tourists
annually. It stretches 1,800 miles (2,897 km) across the Pacific Ocean,
touching the southern, northern, eastern, and western hemispheres all at once.
Making it the world’s only sovereign nation to do so.
Onto other island countries...
The Caribbean is made up of a few dozen islands… or so you’d think.
It actually has around 7,000 islands. We just don’t hear about most of them
because they’re not inhabited. Depending on the source, anywhere from 40, to 50,
to 70 Caribbean islands are permanently inhabited.
Of those, just three islands - Cuba, Haiti,
and the Dominican Republic - hold 75% of the total Caribbean population. The rest are islets,
cays, and other small features with no permanent population.
It’s not just islands; there are myths about the seas themselves, like…
The Dead Sea is a sea
This one seems like it must be true. After all, it’s right there in the name.
Visitors from all over the world flock there to swim in the intensely salty body of water.
But the world-famous destination is actually a landlocked salt lake.
In order to qualify as a sea, it would have to have some outlet into
the world’s oceans. Instead, it is completely surrounded by land.
Another sea myth…
Seas must be bordered by coasts
Not true for one strange sea,
which is located in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean: the Sargasso Sea.
There is no land around it, no island… nothing.
Just a swirling sea formed by a confluence of ocean currents. These currents change the
nature of the Sargasso Sea itself, making it warmer and saltier than the Atlantic
that surrounds it. Observers have also said the Sargasso Sea is unusually calm,
and has a deep blue water that’s different to that of the neighboring Atlantic.
Its most prominent feature is the drifting golden-brown
seaweed that covers the majority of its surface.
Nothing like the sandy beaches of our next myth’s focus…
If you’re in Miami, it probably feels like it’s one of the hottest places you could visit in the
United States. But that’s mostly due to the city’s humidity; not its actual temperature.
Humidity significantly affects how heat is experienced. For example,
a sunny 86-degree (30 Celsius) summer day can feel like 108 degrees (42.2 Celsius) with 95% humidity.
Because even as the rest of the U.S. sweats during the summer,
the temperature in Miami has never gone above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37.8 Celsius). In fact,
for a long time it only hit that triple digit threshold once: on July 21, 1942.
But August 18th, 2026, it hit that ceiling again. So it’s
possible this geography fact might change yet again in the near future.
Let’s zoom out a little…
Even if most people don’t think the split is 50-50, many believe that the populations
of the Northern and Southern Hemisphere are pretty well balanced. Maybe a 60-40.
In fact, 90% of the world’s population lives in the Northern Hemisphere.
The biggest city in the Southern Hemisphere is Sao Paulo, Brazil, which has over 20 million people,
which is pretty impressive. But most of the most populated countries in the world reside entirely,
or almost entirely, in the Northern Hemisphere. This includes China,
India, the USA, Pakistan, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Russia, and Mexico.
Of the top 10 populated countries,
only Brazil and Indonesia are partly in the Southern Hemisphere as well.
At least there are some general facts that must be true, right? Like…
Every country is in the same year
Even if you haven’t thought about this, most people assume it’s true. Why would
different countries around the world be experiencing years differently?
But it’s not actually the case.
Especially in Ethiopia.
There, a year lasts 13 months. The country didn’t adjust to the Gregorian
calendar when it was introduced in 500 A.D, preferring to use the old Coptic calendar.
Time is also calculated differently in general,
as the country uses 2 12-hour periods calculated from dawn to dusk and vice versa.
That means while the rest of the world is in 2026, Ethiopia will be welcoming the new year of 2019.
Geography is full of surprises. And one continent has more than
its fair share. Watch “50 Insane US Geography Facts That Seem Fake But Are
100% Real” to see how wild geography can actually get. Or click on this.
